speechtext:

This, Mr. Speaker, was the case to which I referred the other day. The house may remember that the hon. mem-

ber for North Simcoe (Mr. Boys) and the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), interpreting, I think the spirit of the house, stated that if the facts were in accordance with the extracts from the letter I read they would oppose this bill in committee. Now the trouble is that this bill went to the committee with a whole grist of others. As I understand it, neither the hon. member for North Simcoe nor the hon. member for Lisgar was present in the committee when this went through; nor did I know it was going through until the next morning after we had had' the discussion. I was therefore unable to follow it up before it had passed the committee on private bills. It is for this reason that I take the rather exceptional method, but one quite within the rules, of asking that at this stage we do not press the consideration of this bill but refer it back to our committee for further investigation.
According to the evidence as presented to the senate committee, I notice that this was an uncontested bill. The respondent was not present. The petitioner made certain statements which were corroborated by the statements of tram of his friends. The respondent was said to have lived at a rooming house, with one Arthur Hacking, and that, as far as I read the evidence, is the only direct testimony of her being guilty of the offence alleged. Further than that, the petitioner and his two friends state that the woman made admission of having had improper relations with the correspondent. That is about as far as the evidence before the senate committee goes; and I understand it is customary that when the petition is uncontested there is not a great deal of attention given to further inquiry into the case.
Only a day or so ago I received a second letter from the woman involved. I should gladly have avoided giving any publicity to her name in this connection, but since I am making a plea that this divorce bill be refused I think perhaps the only course I can follow is to take the house into my confidence and read this personal letter. Let me preface it by saying that I have no independent knowledge of the facts in the case. It may very well be that the woman is guilty; I have had no opportunities for making investigation. But I do think that when statements and charges are made, such as are contained in this letter, the least that can be done is to provide that the woman has a chance to be heard. If her allegations prove to be false, very well; if however, they should prove on investigation to be true, then I think that

Procedure in Divorce
we should have done a very gross injustice had we passed a bill of this character without further inquiry. This is the letter:
Mr. Woodsworth,
Member of Parliament,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,
Received your very kind letter for which I thank you sincerely.
I noticed your reference to my letter in the Montreal Star and I wish also to thank you and Mr. Boys for your decision to vote against the bill.
My lawyer received the report of the senate committee the day before I wrote you and your letter has made it quite clear to me that there is no provision for custody of children and it is not within the powers of the federal parliament to deal with questions of alimony.
My first lawyer did not seem to take much interest in my case and the one I have now tells me that the Quebec law is very unsettled as to alimony and guardianship of children when a divorce has been pronounced, because the civil law of this province does not deal with divorce but only with separation as to bed and board.
In any case as you tell me that the federal law cannot help me as to alimony and as 1 have no money to go to Ottawa and appear before any committee, I will ask my lawyer to do everything possible, but I think the child is so young that he could very well be given to me by parliament especially now that circumstances cannot be interpreted as _being unfavourable to me in my way of living.
My husband is trying to make you believe I was living with this man, if I understand the report correctly, but I was living with his mother as a boarder. The little money I did make I gave to Mrs. Hacking with the exception of money for my carfare to work, to keep the home going.
I sold my diamond to pay her rent and now she is trying to keep my few moveable belongings because she says I owe her money. I haven't even my clothes and have not the money to pay to get them. If it were not for these kind people I am with who are willing to wait until I can pay my board, I should be on the street entirely.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether
I should rise to a point of order, but I do not think it is proper to read private letters in this house having regard to a matter which is under consideration here. In view of the fact that my hon. friend is in favour of a divorce court, and since his only objection here is that parliament voted against such a court, I would ask him if he thinks anyone would be allowed to send a judge private letters of this kind, and whether he believes such letters should be read in a court of justice in opposition to the evidence which has been produced.

I know of no rule of this house which prevents me from reading this private letter. As to the propriety of my 78594-128
action, let me say this:	Undoubtedly I
believe in a divorce court; that is my only reason for having taken this matter so seriously, but the Minister of Justice was one of those who prevented the establishment of such a court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My point is that no
judge would permit such a letter to be read in court.

I am sure the Minister of Justice will agree with me that if in reality we are a court we should have the evidence before us, but that is not the case here. The senate committee did not have this information, and in our own private bills committee there was no consideration whatever of the details of this case. I am not putting forward this letter as evidence in the case; I am bringing it before parliament simply as the appeal of a poor woman for a chance to be heard. I ask that we send this case back to our committee where evidence may be heard, and then we will not need to depend upon this letter; we can summon the woman and other witnesses. Let her charges be oarefully sifted. I am simply bringing forward the plea of this woman, and I know of no other way in which I may attain the object desired.

This case was brought to the attention of the house by my hon. friend the other day before the bill was referred to committee. Why did he not take advantage of that opportunity and bring these matters to the attention of the house?

I made an explanation a few minutes ago, but perhaps my hon. friend was not present. This bill was considered by the committee the following morning, when the members of the committee who had spoken in favour of rejecting the bill if the woman's statements were true, the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Boys) and the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), were not present. I was not present either; I did not imagine it would come up so soon. I immediately called the attention of the hon. member for Simcoe to these facts in a letter which I wrote him, and as a matter of fact this fuller information, contained in this second letter, has come to me since that committee met, so I could not have presented this information before the committee. I wrote this woman immediately on receipt of her first letter; subsequently I received this second letter on which I now make an appeal to parliament. I could not have presented the

Procedure in Divorce

second letter before the committee; I did not have it at that time. I think that very well illustrates the fact that because of the hasty way in which we grant these divorces we are not dealing fairly with all the people concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Since my hon. friend
says he knows of no rule which would prevent him from reading the letter I would quote rule 306, page 101 of Beauchesne:
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.

I submit there is
nothing in that rule which is relevant to the matter under discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly the rule applies; my hon. friend says the evidence is not sufficient, and he reads a private letter complaining about the evidence which has been taken with regard to this matter.
Surely the Minister of Justice is not arguing the point seriously.
If my hon. friend is finished with that letter may I see it?

I am not finished with it; I was interrupted while I was reading the letter. I will send my hon. friend a copy later. Now I will finish the letter:
If necessary, I can give the name of the doctor who performed my operation, also the hospital in Ottawa. I do not wish to do this unless it will help materially in my case, as the doctor was wonderful to me professionally and I would not care to give him undue publicity.
I heard my brother-in-law admit he had offered to get Mr. Hacking a good job if he would take me to a hotel and put me in a compromising position in order to get evidence enough for the divorce.
Also he has boasted to me that his brother would never have gone so far as to divorce me if it were not that he had made his brother do it.
He says he worked night and day trying to get evidence. I was grateful for what Arthur Hacking had done in refusing to help their plans so when he requested me to live with him and his mother I readily consented. I thought the money might as well help her as anyone else. I did not realize then that 1 was playing into their hands.
As I was not in Ottawa to defend myself, naturally they had the opportunity to put things in the very worst light possible.
My brother-in-law and his mother kidnapped the baby. He held me while his mother ran out with my baby.
After he was returned to me, my brother-inlaw never let my husband rest until he made him leave me again.
[Mi. Woodsworth.]
Mr. Bourdon refused to listen to me and he and his brother took the child away again.
I told him he could look after the baby better than I could but when I said that I thought he would come back to me.
During our trouble I thought Valmyre would be better away from it all. I did not realize things were as serious as they were. Please believe me when I say if I lose them both, I lose everything worth living for.
I have been very foolish and have done things which seem to be worse than they really are. Since this trouble started I hardly know what I am doing or saying. Arthur Hacking is very revengeful as he has sworn to do everything he can to make me lose my husband and child. He has told Mr. Bourdon some terrible things and he believed because he wants to believe.
I know if he did not get the divorce he would come back to me and I could make him forget all these terrible nine months. Will you not do all you can to give him back to me? Will you not give me the chance to make him forget and be happy once more with our little one? Our child needs most of all his mother, but he loves his daddy and needs him too. I am begging for life itself, will you give it to me?
Perhaps all this seems foolish when read with impersonal eyes but only God knows how my heart is torn for my two loved ones.
Are all my prayers and suffering these nine months to go un-answered and unheard? If it is not possible to do much for me, even a little will be appreciated more than you will ever know. As I said before, you are my last hope.
Please don't let them take my precious baby from me.
Again I thank you sincerely for your kind letter and efforts in my behalf, and shall wait for a favourable answer.
Sincerely.
(Sgd.) Mrs. Antoine Bourdon.
I think that letter makes it own appeal. This woman did not appear before the committee. I understand that if she had made application to the senate committee they would have given an order on her husband compelling him to pay sufficient money to permit her to appear and give her side of the case. Apparently she did not know anything about that; apparently the lawyer whom she consulted was very indifferent and did not inform her of her position. In any case, the matter came before the senate committee and she was not present; all the evidence was received from one side, from the petitioner and two of his personal friends. Under our procedure this matter has gone through the various stages until now it has passed our own committee, where it received no consideration of any kind. This is the last opportunity to do anything in the matter, hence the rather unusual procedure I have been forced to adopt. I cannot think that any member of this house will deliberately deny this woman the chance to be heard, and that is all I ask. She may be an imposter; she may be guilty; it may be that her statements

Procedure in Divorce
are quite untrue. It may be that her charges with regard to the illegal operation are not well founded; I do not know nor am I in position to know, and I do not think anyone can know until she is called before our committee to prove her charges. I do not know whether our committee has ever investigated a case in this manner before, but I am quite sure it has the right to advance money to the women for her expenses. If the senate committee could have ordered the husband to advance money to bring his wife here to appear in her own behalf I do not know why our committee cannot do the same. In this case I am not holding up the business of the house because of the general procedure at all, but because I consider it a serious matter and one in which the rights of a citizen of this country are not being safeguarded, and I appeal to the house to permit an investigation by our own committee before we take a vote on this bill.

I rise to express the hope that the house will permit this bill to be sent back for reconsideration by the private bills committee. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) brought this case to the attention of the house the other day, and I determined to do the best I could to have this matter investigated by the committee. However, for some reason or other, I did not receive my notification for the meeting of the committee. I do not suggest for a moment there was anything deliberate in that, I am sure it was purely an accident, but the fact remains that I did not receive that notice and hence I was not at the committee and had not the opportunity to direct the attention of the committee to this particular case. The hon. member is only asking that this woman be heard before our committee and that we ourselves judge her claim; I think that is a fair request. It has been said, and I believe it is true, that the expenses of this woman can be paid in order to permit her to give evidence in her own behalf.
She had an opportunity to appear before the senate committee.

So far as I know this woman had no opportunity to appear before any committee, and I do not think she was aware of the fact that she could appear and have her expenses paid. Having no money herself she evidently did not know that dhe could make application for her expenses.
She must have been notified.

I do not know anything about notification. As the hon. member for 78594-128J
Winnipeg North Centre has said, the only thing to do is to bring the woman before the committee and investigate the case.

If there is any doubt in the mind of any hon. member as to the facts not having been proven, or that there are any additional facts which should be brought out,
I certainly have no objection to it going back to the committee.

I wish to move an amendment to this bill, notice of which was given some days ago, as follows:
That section 1 of the bill be amended by adding the following words thereto:
"and the said Florence Velma Strachan have the custody of their child William Swinton Strachan, and that the said Alexander Swinton Strachan shall pay annually to Florence Velma Strachan for her support and maintenance the sum of five hundred dollars, so long as she remains unmarried, and the sum of two hundred dollars annually for the support and education of their child William Swinton Strachan."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As this amendment
raises a question of constitutional law questions, I must ask the hon. gentleman to let it stand until the matter is given proper study. It is a question which might be held to interfere with civil rights of those residing in the different provinces, and I would like some time to consider the question before giving a ruling as to whether or not the amendment is in order.

May I point out
that this notice was given several days ago, and is quite regular. The proposal is advanced in this particular bill simply in order that this may be a test case. We took the first bill that seemed to be suitable, and if this amendment is in order and if legislation of this kind is within the competence of parliament, we propose to move similar amendments in connection with other bills. It does not seem fair that you, Mr. Chairman, should ask that this stand and that we should proceed to other bills where we would then have no opportunity whatever of making similar amendments. As the Chairman knows, we have to give notice before amendments can be made. We thought this would be a test case. Now you say that you reserve your decision whether or not the amendment is in order, and yet you wish us to go on with other bills. I do not think that is quite fair to those of us who are anxious to expedite business but who nevertheless desire to insist that it be given due consideration. If this amendment that we provide for the support of the children and alimony for the wife, is in order, then it ought to be placed in every bill of this character right down the list. If

you, Mr. Chairman, let this case stand and then go on with the other bills, we would be quite in order to ask that other bills of this character should also stand until this principle is decided.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Has the wife asked for
that provision for alimony?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. members are
doing this out of the kindness of their hearts.

As is known; alimony was granted and the support of the children provided for only in the first cases brought before the Canadian House of Commons. It has not been the custom to ask for this, and in the ordinary petitions it is not included. The women in such cases do not know they have the privilege of asking for it, and the lawyers do not so inform them. Indeed, the lawyers do not know; no one knows, as a matter of fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But if we granted this,
we would be granting more than the petition asked for.

Yes, but why not? If there is a case of substantial injustice: if a woman has married in good faith and if for some reason her husband proves to be a worthless fellow or unfaithful to her, and after some years deserts her, she is thrown upon the world with no opportunity whatever of providing a living for herself. Marriage has at least some elements of a civil contract, and a wife under those circumstances ought to have some claim upon her husband. It is within the competence of this house to grant or not to grant this divorce; it is also within the power of the house to say under what conditions that divorce shall be granted. That can be done whether or not we go beyond the original terms of the petition.

I should like to
be quite clear upon what authority my hon. friend suggests that the house is empowered to make any such order as is now sought. I cannot get the authority for it.

I am not a lawyer. My hon. friend is a lawyer and probably he knows more about the legal side of the matter than I do. I must confess that I am relying largely on the general principles of justice. But I would point out that divorces are not being granted under statutory provisions; that there is no law under which we are acting in this matter; that it is the common law of Great Britain, and that we are simply following precedent. I am subject to correction,

Procedure in Divorce
but I understand that it is competent for parliament to grant divorce for any reason whatsoever. It has been customary to grant divorce only on the ground of unfaithfulness or impotence. I think those are the only two grounds that have been recognized by the house, but I do not see any reason why we should not go beyond them. In other words, there is no statutory limitation, therefore I suggest it is open to us to say under what terms the divorce shall be granted. I submit that it is quite within our power to refuse divorce until such time as suitable provision is made for the children and the wife.

How are we to
know that?

We are discovering that we have no knowledge with regard to these matters. The evidence given before the senate committee does not reveal to us whether the wife has an independence or not; it does not reveal to us who is to take care of the children or whether the mother to whom the children are left is capable of caring for them. Under those circumstances, it seems to me that we in this house have a perfect right at least to make inquiries concerning the circumstances of the wife and children before proceeding to grant a divorce.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Does the
amendment of the hon. member for Rosetown not provide for alimony and for the custody of the children?
Yes.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
It is quite
a different thing from what my hon. friend is arguing for. The amendment interferes with property and civil rights, but the hon. member is not arguing on that ground at all.

If the hon. member had followed me closely, I said that I thought we were within our rights; at least that we were following the precedent of the first case dealt with in the House of Commons if we provided for alimony and for the support of the children. That was done in the Campbell case, and that case has never been contested in the courts.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am not
denying that, but I think my hon. friend would be on stronger ground if he would confine his argument to his proposal, namely, that the house do not act until assured alimony will be granted.

Well, we may proceed in that way later on. In the meantime I suggest that since the action in the Campbell case has never been contested in the courts, we are on fairly safe ground in following that precedent. I was further answering the hon. member for West Hamilton when I said that there lay, even beyond that, the right of insisting that a divorce should not be granted until such time as adequate provision could be made for the wife and the children involved.

It must not be forgotten
that divorce bills are sent to the house by people wishing to be exempted from the general law. The general law in Ontario and Quebec is the indissolubility of the marriage tie. These people come here and ask for a favour; they ask for special reasons, to be relieved from the operation of the general act. We deal with each particular case, but according to Bourinot it has been held in the past:
In case, however, the house is not satisfied with the evidence on which the senate has passed the bill, it is always competent for the committee on private bills to go into such further examination of the facts as may be deemed desirable in the interests of justice and society.
I am opposed to divorce on principle, but in this case the hon. gentleman has certainly the right to ask that these bills be dealt with according to the principle of justice. If there are children born of any marriage, and if the applicant wants to be relieved from the obligations which he contracts when he becomes married, some way should be provided by which he may not be permitted to throw his wife and children out on the street without making provision for them. That is a matter of elementary justice.
This question of divorce is essentially a matter that affects civil rights, just as marriage does, and both marriage and property come within the purview of the province. The fathers of confederation, not desiring to implant divorce on Ontario and Quebec as it existed in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, but not knowing what to do with the child found on the doorstep, said: We will relegate this matter to the central authority to make it more and more difficult for divorce to take place in this country. The results showed that they were wise in their generation, for during the first ten years after confederation only seven divorces were granted by this parliament, and up until 1879, special committees were appointed by the House of Commons to deal with each case. But what
Procedure in Divorce

do we see to-day? There have been 293 applications for divorce during this present session, and there are 80 divorce bills on this order paper for to-day. I think the time has come, therefore, when it is the duty of the House of Commons to look into this matter more closely with a view to discouraging people from applying to parliament for divorce, and to discourage the belief that all that it is necessary to do to secure a divorce is merely to send in an application and the divorce will be granted without any answer from the respondent. I hope that some means will 'be found next session to remedy this great evil. I do not want to delay the house on this bill to discuss the principle of divorce, but I may say that I was pleased to see in Saturday's Journal a pronouncement by the Church of England in Canada on this very question. It declares that divorce is the outstanding question for the Canadian people to deal with to-day. It reiterates the stand which that church has previously taken and calls on all its clergymen to bring this very important question to the attention of their people, and not to re-marry people who have been divorced either by the courts or by parliament. I was glad, I say, to see this pronouncement by the Church of England in Canada, because it shows that public opinion in this country is being awakened with respect to this matter.

I do not know the
facts in this particular case, but apparently this woman believes that she is obtaining through parliament the redress to which she is entitled. We do not know at this time whether or not she desires an order for alimony against her husband, or whether she has the custody of the children, if there are any. But under this bill she is obtaining the redress that she has asked for, and while I am quite agreeable to the bill going back to the private bills committee for reconsideration, I do not think we have power to pass such an amendment as has been proposed. I do not believe it is within the competence of this house to make an order granting alimony to a person who has not asked for it, if indeed it is possible for us to grant alimony at all. It would appear to me to come under the heading of civil rights, and would therefore be under the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature. I think it would be better if the amendment were drafted in such a way that the bill be referred back to the private bills committee to reconsider the case; otherwise this woman may be deprived entirely of the divorce which she

desires, and possibly rightly desires. If we have to act upon this particular amendment, it may mean that instead of the petitioner being granted what she has asked for, she may 'be denied any remedy whatever. I would therefore suggest that the amendment be altered so that the effect will simply be to refer the bill back to the private bills committee.

May I inquire of the
sponsor of this bill who 'has the custody of the children, whether it is the father, the mother, or anyone else?

The petitioner who is applying for this divorce has the custody of the child and seems to be quite satisfied to look after her own child. I agree with the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Bothwell) that the question of alimony is one for the civil courts; under chapter 184 of the revised statutes of Ontario, being the Deserted Wives' and Children's Maintenance Act, subsections 1 and 2, page 1904, redress to the petitioner may be given. I believe the motion of the hon. member for Rosetown is out of order. This bill was sent back before on the very same ground that it is now proposed to send it back. As far as I am concerned, I want to see everything done that can possibly be done for the child, but the petitioner seems satisfied to look after her own child, and she has as much right to look after her own child as the father.

The amendment was moved in good faith, in the belief that we had the power to deal with this matter. I still believe that if parliament has the power to grant divorces, which is a most serious matter as between two married persons, it should have the power to say on what terms that separation shall be granted. The sponsor of the bill has told us that the woman has the custody of the child, but evidently he does not know whether she has t'he necessary means for its support. We know nothing about this case. Surely we have the right to amend these bills as they come before us. If we have not, then I say that the granting of divorce by parliament is simply a farce, and we have carried it on much too long. But as the suggestion has been made that the bill be referred back to t'he private bills committee, I have no objection, although I do not see that there is any need for it.

The object, as I understand it, is to provide a test case to ascertain if we really have the power to grant alimony. If the amendment carries and we are later advised by the law officers that we have not

the power, then the question will be settled so far as parliament is concerned. When I was speaking on this very question some time ago, the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) took directly the opposite view to that which has been expressed here to-day, he said that parliament has power to deal with this matter, that parliament has actually granted alimony. I think it would be well to bring up a test case to see whether or not that power is intra vires of this parliament.

I would like to submit to my hon. friends that that is not the proper way to bring a matter of importance of this character to a legal test, simply to move an amendment to a bill in the House of Commons. In the first place, the absurdity-I was going to say-of the position we now find ourselves in is this, that the party has already the custody of the child which we are now solemnly asking parliament to give.
I submit that that is really not the right way to proceed. The whole thing arises out of a difference of opinion among the members of this house, in the first place, on the principle of divorce, and secondly, as to the procedure under which divorce has been granted by parliament for a number of years. I have listened here for weeks now to very lengthy addresses by hon. members, particularly by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre, my hon. friend from Labelle, and others, in which it seemed to be implied that those of us who have been more or less silent are entirely in favour of divorce being granted in a most reckless manner. I wish to say, and I feel impelled to say this by the continuity of these debates, that as far as I am concerned I am absolutely opposed to divorce. That is my personal feeling, but I do not come to parliament merely to give expression to my personal views on matters of this kind. I realize that it is accepted throughout the Dominion that divorce may be granted. The practice in two or three provinces has been to grant them through a petition to this parliament and an act being passeed; in other provinces, divorce is granted by the courts. It does not seem to me that we are discharging our duty properly, simply because we have personal prejudices in this matter, to seek to interfere with the redress that other people claim is their right as citizens. I admit to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre that it may appear to some that the manner in which divorce has been granted by parliament has been, we will say, somewhat rapid, but I do feel that he has been a little unfair, in fact I think very unfair, to the senate committee, because my experience in the last twenty sessions is that the senate
Procedure in Divorce
committee, of all the committees of parliament of either house, has given its time to the consideration of its duties, and given it ungrudgingly, and I think to most, if not all, of the members the work has been most distasteful. Therefore I think it is rather unfair to them to be constantly insinuating, or at least leaving the impression in the minds of the public, that that committee is a callous body without any particular consideration for the rights of women and children, and that it deals with the petitions carelessly and recklessly. For instance, my hon. friend moved a certain bill back to committee a few moments ago. I sent out for the evidence and I have been reading it, and I must say that I can see very little reason to question the decision of the senate committee. However, we are quite willing, if a member brings forward the question of the safeguarding of the rights of one of the parties to the suit, to give further opportunity for dealing with it.
But coming to the matter immediately before us, I do not think that this parliament, without much consideration, should immediately adopt a system of granting alimony and the custody of children, when these matters are not cited in the petition, and when it has not been the practice of parliament to deal with them, and when we know that in the provinces there is a very elaborate procedure set up whereby deserted wives and mothers may obtain redress, and children be cared for. I do not think that as a matter of theory or to further some idea of abstract justice we should plunge into these matters and give a decision without consideration.
I do not think my hon. friend is correct. This is only a test case and the hon. leader of the opposition said parliament has the right to grant alimony.

I think in this case it is abstract justice. I believe I quote my hon. leader's opinion corectly when I say he holds that parliament, having the right to grant divorce, has also a perfect right to deal with all matters that arise out of the granting of divorce-the Minister of Justice might agree that that is a sound principle of law-and perhaps had done so in the past. But we are not calling that in question. For years and years a certain practice has been followed, and the Prime Minister declared the other day-I think a little tardily, his declaration should have been made last session; however, he did so, and with a degree of graciousness that my hon. friend ought to recognize- he declared that the government would take this very difficult problem into consideration and endeavour to find some solution.
Procedure in Divorce

Now my hon. friend is asking me to vote cn an amendment which frankly we are not in a position to discuss. The proper place to have raised the question would have been before the senate committee when the case was first considered. It was not raised there, it does not appear in the petition, and it occurs to me that my hon. friends would do well to let this testing of a principle, as they describe it, be considered and determined in connection with the whole question which we understand the government is now going to take into consideration. I think it rather too bad that my hon. friends have felt that the course taken by them was necessary. I agree it is a pity that the government did not last year take notice of the accumulation of these cases, and endeavour to lead parliament into some solution of the difficulty of the administration of this branch of law. I am not saying that by way of censure of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only solution that was proposed was rejected by the house.
I quite agree with my hon. friend; but it has been shown by the discussion in the house that the problem is still here.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I know.
Mr- STEVENS: The Prime Minister has i old us very frankly that he recognizes that the problem exists, and he is going to find some way of adjusting the difficulty. I do not think my hon. friend Should ask the house to deal with what I again say is an abstract principle of justice. It is not involved in this bill, the petitioner does not ask for it; therefore it is merely a question of whether we should carry on the practice in this way or not. The whole subject is to be considered by the government, and personally I do not think we should be asked to give an opinion on it at the present time.

The hon. member for Vancouver Centre said that at the present time the mother has charge of the child. The amendment asks that the mother shall have charge of the child legally. To-day there is nothing to prevent the husband from taking the child away.
How does my hon. friend know that?
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre earlier this afternoon pointed out a case where a child was forcibly taken away from the mother. Therefore I think there is some reason in the amendment.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: As I pointed out to my hon. friend a few moments ago, Mr. Chairman, if it were a mere matter of objecting to the passage of this particular bill on the grounds that alimony and the custody of the child or children had not been decided, one could understand the motion, but to make a motion for these specific purposes-something which we have never been asked to express an opinion on, during the period that I have been in this house, at all events-in my humble opinion is an attempt to do that which is outside our jurisdiction. Moreover, the courts are available for the dealing with the question of the custody of the children or child. If one of the parents is deemed to be immoral, the court in every case that I have heard of, has made the other parent the custodian. The same procedure applies to alimony. This woman is not necessarily debarred from the courts of her own province if she desires to secure alimony. I do not think parliament is in possession of all the facts to deal with these matters.

It appears to me that when these petitioners come before parliament seeking divorce they come well advised. I notice they are represented by very eminent counsel, some great constitutional authorities, strange as it may seem, representing certain of the petitioners. It stands to reason that they have given due consideration to the rights of the petitioners and they have asked for all ihat they believe parliament can grant. If the mover of this amendment wishes to have the powers enlarged we cannot enlarge them by voting on the present proposal. It seems to me that parliament should have a definition of the legal rights of petitioners for divorce; and that definition-as to the right for instance of parliament to grant alimony or to decide with respect to the custody of the children-should come from the legal department and not be inferred from a vote in this house. I think the hon. member who moved the amendment will agree that parliament is not a body competent to give a legal opinion. Parliament relies on the Department of Justice for its legal opinions, and in this instance, in my opinion at least, if there is anything to be explained the explanation should come from that department. The explanation should not be gathered from the result of a vote in this committee.

I am opposed to divorce on principle, but as regards a definition with respect to the granting of alimony and the decision as to the custody of children I do

Procedure in Divorce
not see any reason why this parliament, if it has the right to grant divorces, should not have the right also to consider these other questions. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), who probably is better posted on the subject than I am-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

-made the statement that alimony was a civil right and that a woman getting a divorce could go to the civil courts if she wished to obtain alimony. But I would point out that if we dissolve a marriage here no right can exist in the matter of alimony for the simple reason that, after the dissolution by this parliament, there is no state of marriage in relation to the parties concerned; therefore there can be no civil right as regards alimony so far as the courts are concerned. After we have dissolved a marriage here how can the woman go to a civil court to get alimony?-there is no marriage. The only condition under which alimony can be granted is when the divorce is granted by the civil courts.

I thought it was
suggested that the Minister of Justice would speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, he remains as silent as he can.

After the divorce is
granted here has the woman the privilege to go to the civil court in order to establish her claim in regard to alimony? The hon. member (Mr. Beaubien) has brought out this point and it seems to me the Minister of Justice should favour us with an expression of opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should like to have
the question stand as a notice. So far as the province of Quebec is concerned, with the conditions in which I am more familiar, I know that alimony can be obtained in the courts. Of course, there is no divorce there. The chairman, I think, has indicated a wish to reserve decision on the motion which has been made, and we have been discussing this matter an hour since he so intimated. Would it not be well to leave it at that pending his decision, after he has received advice from the proper source?

WThat about the
subsequent bills?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
intend to make a similar motion in regard to every bill-not only to grant divorce to those who seek it but also to give them money for which they do not ask?
If this is intra vires and we are in harmony with the rules of procedure, I think it would be only right that inquiry should be made in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To grant them alimony even if they do not ask for it? The hon. gentleman is over generous.

I said that inquiry
should be made in each case; I was explicit on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But if they do not ask
for it why make an investigation? Why investigate whether they want it or not?

Because in the
past we have not been fair to the women in these provinces. The women of Ontario and Quebec have not had the opportunity of bringing their rights before any court where those rights can be properly investigated, and at the present moment we are simply pleading that in some way provision shall be made that women seeking divorces will not be thrown on the street and their children left to shift for themselves. If this bill is to stand until the Chairman reaches a decision, I do not wish to see other bills prevented from going through. But I wish to add some further considerations.
It has been said that it is open to the woman who is granted a divorce to enter action afterwards in the civil courts. I understand however that the trouble is that it is very difficult to get the civil courts to give a decision in such matters. I believe it is the general principle that the same court that grants a divorce ought to arrange the provisions under which that divorce is granted; and certainly there should not be the added expense, imposed upon poor people when they come to this parliament and obtain a divorce, of having to go on later to the civil courts to obtain the custody of children or to secure arrangements for their maintenance. I think it is quite proper that the rights of parliament should be defined, as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Clark) has suggested. But how is that to be arranged? This matter has been brought up again and again, and always we are met with the answer given by the Minister of Justice-"we will take it into consideration."

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought my hon. friend was pleased the other day when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) suggested
Procedure in Divorce

that the government be given an opportunity until next session to look into the matter. The hon. gentleman declared himself satisfied. But now he starts the whole discussion over again.

The Prime Minister the other day stated that during the present session the house had decided against a divorce court for Ontario and that for that reason the question could not again be considered at this time. It was on that ground that some of us accepted his assurances. I have no doubt whatever that the Prime Minister spoke in good faith, believing that to be the situation. But after consulting the authorities I find that there is no reason why the matter may not be introduced at this session. It would be well, therefore, that the house should be clear on the situation. We are willing to let the matter stand if nothing else can be done. But if the question can be decided at this session it should be decided and not postponed, and thus an unsatisfactory procedure maintained in all these cases to be dealt with this year, and with the certainty of the difficulty arising again next year. Let me read from May 13 edition, page 299:
When bills have ultimately passed or have been rejected, the rules of both houses are positive that they shall not be introduced again: but the practice is not strictly in accordance with them. The principle was thus stated bv the Lords. 17th May. 1606-
That when a bill hath been brought into the house, and rejected, another bill of the same argument and matter may not be renewed and begun again in the same house in the same session where the former bill was begun. . ."
That is the senate, in this instance.
"...but if a bill begun in one of the houses, and there allowed and passed, be disliked and refused in the other, a new bill of the same matter may be drawn and begun again in that house whereunto it was sent: and if. a bill being begun in either of the houses, and committed, it be thought by the committees that the matter may better proceed by a new bill, it is likewise holden agreeable to order in such case, to draw a new bill, and to bring it into the house."
Then follows a great number of instances covering a considerable period of time and coming down very nearly to the present. That simply means that under the procedure of our parliament, the senate having brought in this bill and it having been rejected by the House of Commons before a good many of the members knew just what was involved in its rejection, it is still open to us to reconsider our position. Further, now that members of the cabinet have stated very definitely that the present procedure is a farce; now that to-day we have another member of the cabinet saying that we in this house could not possibly 
know the conditions affecting the cases under consideration; now that the Prime Minister has declared the present procedure unsatisfactory and has stated his willingness to bring in some remedial legislation, it seems to me high time that we should insist on some action being taken at the earliest opportunity.
Let me tell the Minister of Justice that I was satisfied with the advance we made the other day, as I then considered it impossible for us to do anything further this session, but since my attention has been called to the fact that under the rules of this parliament it is quite possible for the government to introduce suitable legislation at this session, I am not quite so well satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What legislation?
There is no reason why legislation could not be introduced similar to the bill which was rejected, providing for the establishment of a divorce court in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Surely my hon. friend
knows that the bill to which he refers has been rejected by the house, and that is the end of that bill for this session. Even if his interpretation of the rule were correct would he think it fair to impose his views on the majority of the members of this parliament? Majority must rule, even when that majority does not include my hon. friend.

Quite so; the Minister of Justice need not become sarcastic in discussing the matter. I stated that according to the rules of this house it is quite within our competence to introduce that very bill again, and I think the temper of the house is such that another vote on the question might be very different from the vote we took some time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is flattering himself; he has not succeeded in convincing the house to that extent.

Then I was going to suggest that there might be other methods available. For instance, it has been suggested that it might be possible to refer the responsibility for granting divorces to the exchequer court. I know some members of the senate have been considering the advisability of empowering the exchequer court, which is a court of parliament, to undertake the investigation of or perhaps actually to recommend or grant divorces. If I understand the situation correctly, we have it within our power to charge a court to do what we want done. I think it is quite within the powers of this parliament to take that action.

Personally I do not think that would be nearly so satisfactory as the creation of a divorce court for Ontario, but I would say that by so doing we would meet many of the objections which have been raised to the establishment of such a court. In the first place it is clearly within our powers to take such action, and in the second place we would not have to wait until Ontario has expressed an opinion with regard to the matter, as some members have suggested should be done. That is one possible line of action that the government might take even during this session. With these suggestions, I do not think we have yet exhausted the possibilities of action to relieve the situation; therefore I would call the attention of the Minister of Justice and the government to the possibility of proceeding along these lines before this parliament prorogues.

I am so much
in sympathy with the general principle which my hon. friend for Winnipeg North Centre has been advocating for some time with regard to the proper forum in which petitions for divorce should be considered that it is with considerable regret that I am compelled to differ from him now. However, in connection with the matter now under consideration I desire to direct the attention of the house to this fact:	Almost from
time immemorial questions affecting certain domestic relations, questions of alimony, of the custody of children and so on, have engaged the attention of the leading courts in the British Empire, and it has been well recognized that only by those who have engaged in a lifetime of study and investigation of the law and of special cases has it been possible to reach decisions which are worthy of that law which we desire to see upheld. maintopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext:
Authority is
sought to construct, improve, fnaintain and operate a combined canal and ship channel or deep waterway from a point below the city of Sorel to a point near Cornwall of not less than thirty-five feet for the passage of ocean-going vessels. The route of the proposed canal is to be from Sorel to Montreal, from Montreal to Laprairie basin, and from Laprairie basin to Cornwall. It is proposed as an alternative to improve and make navigable for ocean navigation the Richelieu river from Sorel to Chambly basin and to construct a suitable canal from Chambly basin to a point on the southeast shore of Laprairie basin. In view of the wide powers asked for in this bill. I think the best way will be to give it second reading and refer it to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, where all the necessary information incidental to the project may be made available.
Hon. II. H. STEVENS (Vancouver Centre):
I am not desirous, Mr. Speaker, of opposing an application for the consideration of any reasonable project, but I submit that this bill is of grave importance. The powers asked for are of a very extensive character, and will affect directly the great St. Lawrence project which is now occupying the attention of the government of Canada and the governments of the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Only recently the federal government approved of certain plans under the Navigable Waters Act with respect to the Beauhamois scheme, which involves the construction by a private corporation of a canal as well as a power plant. This will vitally affect those great projects. If we give this bill second reading it will of course be said that we have agreed to the principle of the bill. I notice the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) shakes his head, but I am stating what is actually the fact so far as parliament is concerned. Undoubtedly, when a bill of this character is brought forward we are supposed to consider on the second reading its broad general principle, in this case whether parliament is to agree to a private corporation constructing a series of canals in the St. Lawrence. I do not want my hon. friend, the sponsor of the bill, to think that I am merely captious in my criticism, but, speaking for myself, I am not prepared to agree now to the principle of any private corporation undertaking the improvement of the St. Lawrence waterway. I think almost from confederation the question of the canalization of the St. Lawrence to the great lakes has been in the hands of the parliament of Canada. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent by the people of Canada on this great work. I think we ought not to give this bill second reading. Probably the government should have taken the whole question into consideration and have been prepared, when the bill came forward, to state their attitude in regard to it. It should not be the duty of any private member, especially on the opposition side, to now offer objections to the bill, because after all it is a question for parliament and particularly for the government to consider. If the government are prepared to endorse the bill publicly, then it becomes a question of policy whether we shall get behind or oppose the government in the matter. Speaking for myself, I am opposed to the principle of a private corporation being granted the powers set forth in this bill.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr.iSpeaker,I should have spoken immediately after the sponsor of the bill (Mr. Smith) moved the second reading had not my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) been on his feet. With most of his remarks I am in cordial agreement. I for one am not convinced that there should be such a canal as is proposed in this bill, and certainly the government is not adopting the principle of permitting private corporations to enter into the business of canalization and charging tolls, when it has been the policy of successive governments for a great many years past to operate, for the marine traffic of this country, canals without any toll charges. The question which arises in connection with the bill is one which has been frequently referred to this house. When private parties petition for private legislation and pay the fees demanded by this house it is presumed that they will get an opportunity themselves to present the object in which they are interested and for which they desire parliamentary approval. There is only one place where petitioners can thus appear, and that is before one of the select standing committees of this house. That is the only reason why I should be prepared personally to vote for the second reading of this bill-in order that those concerned may have an opportunity of presenting to a committee of this house such arguments as are in their possession, such information as they have, which would warrant parliament in

speechtext: Does the second reading of a private bill necessarily commit this hou-'e to the principle of the bill?

maintopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY LIMITED
speechtext: That of course is very debatable in connection with a private bill. But if my hon. friend puts his question in this form: Does the second reading of a private bill, which necessarily involves its reference to a committee of the house for its examination, commit this house to the final passage of the bill?-I can answer him definitely in the negative. It merely involves, in my judgment,-and I speak only as one member of the house-that the house in passing the second reading of the bill permits the petitioners to appear in the only way they can appear, before a select committee, there to endeavour to make out their case. I have indicated that personally I am opposed to the bill as such; but I see no way of treating petitioners fairly, after they have paid their fees, than at least to give them a hearing. That may not 6uit hon. gentlemen; I know it does not. But personally I have consistently followed that course-and, as I say, I speak only for myself in the matter. Certainly I do not deem myself voting for the passage of the bill in voting for the second reading; not at all; in fact, it would require a great deal of new information to persuade me that it is worth voting for at all. maintopic: GREAT LAKES AND ATLANTIC CANAL AND POWER COMPANY LIMITED

I would not trespass on tlhe time of the house were it not for the observations of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning). It is laid down in May clearly that when the house gives second reading to a private bill it approves the principle of the bill. It approves the principle, although the details of the measure may be considered in the committee to which it may be referred.
What is the principle of this bill? The principle of this bill is that a private company may construct a canal and charge tolls, undertake hydro-electric enterprises, construct bridges, and enter upon various matters of that kind. It takes some thirteen pages to outline the provisions of the bill. The Minister of Railways, whose department is directly affected, has said that the petitioner's have given their notice and paid the advertising fees and the fees due to the clerks of the House of Commons and the Senate, and therefore the bill, in his opinion, should go to the committee. I submit with all deference that the principle is that the house itself must determine whether or not it will change a principle which heretofore has been approved, and this house only should vote upon that principle, and not a committee of the house. The house should be convinced, and not a committee. In other words, if the hon. gentleman who introduces the bill is unable to prove to the house in his opening that the matter is one of such great public interest as would warrant this house in departing from the principle which heretofore has guided it in legislation of this character, the bill should not pass. He has not given any explanation to warrant any such thing being done, and as the matter now stands when we give second reading to the bill we have approved the principle of a private canal being constructed, paralleling the St. Lawrence river, with a depth of thirty-five feet and width of four hundred feet, and involving the possibility of tolls being charged, together with various other matters of that kind. I for one will recall to the house what is laid down by May with respect to private bills of this character. When you approve the principle of legislation it must then be assumed that some sort of bill will emerge from the committee to which that legislation is referred. The place to kill the bill, if you wish to kill it, is here and not in the committee; because having sent the bill to the committee you have indicated that you are in favour of the principle of a privately-owned canal, and you instruct the committee to prepare a measure accordingly, and if

Georgian bay canal bill. After lengthy discussion, and after attention had been drawn to what May has to say on the question, the bill finally went to the committee where, when it was considered, not a single member but one was found to vote for it. What happened was this: It occupied weeks of debate in this house and was given second reading, a very persistent lobby having been maintained to secure its second reading. The last minister who spoke upon it was the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler). When the bill reached the committee, however, one member stood up in favour of it. The house was then in the anomalous position of having voted by a majority for the principle of the building of the Georgian bay canal, although, when the bill reached the committee, there was just one hon. member who was loyal to his principles and who stood up for the principle of the bill being given effect to by legislation. If we have no desire to pass this legislation-and apparently we have not-I think the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Smith) will be well advised to take the nays and yeas as indicating whether or not it is the intention of parliament to depart from the principle which has heretofore governed, namely, that canals of this character should be publicly owned and that no tolls should be chargeable in relation thereto. With all my friendly regard for the hon. member for Stormont, I beg to assure him that legislation is not based upon considerations of friendship when it affects the public weal, and I for one propose accordingly to vote against the bill.

Perhaps the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) will see that these reports are brought down before we discuss certain resolutions now appearing on the order paper. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is also interested in these matters in view of the report made by the audit board last year upon the affairs of the harbour commission of Quebec.
I mention this so that when the Minister of Marine and Fisheries reads Hansard to-morrow he will see what we desire.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
The first item is vote No. 131,
harbours and rivers.
As some of the members desire to speak with reference to certain items in vote 132, could this vote be taken up first?

It makes no difference to me.
Charlottetown-reconstruction of railway wharf, $48,000.

Would the
minister give us some information as to the work which is being carried on here?
This is a revote from last year.

Does the
amount cover the rebuilding of the property which was destroyed by fire last year?
2040	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-PHI.
Yes, that is my understanding.

It is very
difficult for the people of Prince Edward Island to understand why the rebuilding of this shed has been delayed so long.

Will the hon. -member
speak just a little louder and will my other hon. friends endeavour to keep a little order, because I cannot hear a word of what is being said?

There was a great deal of dissatisfaction throughout the province in connection with the delay in rebuilding this shed last year. The shed was destroyed some time during June and the rebuilding was not undertaken in time to make it available for the fall season. The people interested think that this delay was unnecessarily long and that the department should have taken some quicker action in order to make the building available for the fall traffic. I am not criticizing the vote in any way except to say that in a matter of such great public interest more energetic measures should have been taken to have the rebuilding done at once.

I have not the correspondence before me but my recollection is that the fire took place some time after the house rose. There was no money in the estimates to provide for the rebuilding and a governor general's warrant had to be obtained at the earliest possible moment. As I recollect, that was done and it is a great surprise to me to h-ear the hon. member say that the work was not proceeded with. I believe I have something among my papers which shows that the representatives down -there have expressed their great appreciation of the expedition with which the department acted in regard to this matter.

We notice
here in the House of Commons and in other places that all the representatives for some of the counties in Prince Edward Island do is to express appreciation to the government for what it happens to do. I have no further objection to the vote.

Item agreed to.
Souris harbour-breakwater repairs, $60,000.

Would the
minister give us some information as to what work was done last year? There was $30,000 voted for this work a year ago and apparently only about $7,000 was expended. The vote has been doubled to $60,000 and I think some explanation would be in order.

The amount of $60,000
is required to complete the work now under contract with Mr. H. J. Phillips of Charlottetown, P.E.I. This contract consists of placing some 1,500 cubic yards of stone, -from two to three cubic yards in size, in front of the outer block, and placing a further quantity of 2,500 cubic yards, from one to two cubic yards in size along the seaward face of middle section of the breakwater for a length of 460 feet. The tot-al amount of stone to be placed is approximately 4,000 cubic yards. The amount expended last year to the 31st March was $8,347.57.
Was this contract made with Mr. Phillips last year?
Yes.
Involving the whole $GO,000 expenditure?
Yes.

This looks like a very large amount of money -to which, of course, I cannot object, and I am not objecting, as it is being spent in my constituency, but the condition of the railway wharf at the same point and right alongside this breakwater, is very serious at the present time. To my mind, better service would be given to the community and to the town of Souris if a portion of this vote were made applicable to some repairs to the railway wharf. It is rather important because it is a transfer point for a large quantity of freight for the Magdalen islands. The shed on the railway wharf is in bad condition; the roof is leaking, and the merchandise that is being transshipped by the railway should be stored there until the boat calls for it. It cannot be stored there at the present time because it would be in danger of destruction on account of the leaky roof. In addition to that, farmers and business men have to store merchandise waiting for the steamer for the Magdalen islands and under present conditions the wharf cannot be used to any extent because goods cannot be protected from the weather on account of the -condition of the roof. It would be better if an additional appropriation could be made for repairs to the railway wharf shed, but if the government cannot see its way clear to provide any more money, as only a small amount was expended last year and as it might not be necessary to spend the whole of the vote this year on the breakw'ater, I would suggest that a part of the appropriation be used to repair the shed. If that were done, there would be more real value given to the

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-P.EJ.
community and better service given to the town, especially in view of the fact that this shed is the only place where stuff can be stored for shipment to the Magdalen islands or to any other port.

Our instructions from the engineers are quite in accord with my hon. friend's statement made to the house a year ago, namely, that the matter which is urgent is the building of the breakwater. The other structures are in danger of being completely destroyed unless the breakwater is constructed. It is the protection for the rest, and the information that I have at hand is thait it should be proceeded with first of all.

Item agreed to.
