speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee rose at six o'clock we were considering vote No. 132. The item we are now considering reads:
Victoria-wharf repairs, $1,100.

I am not sure, Mr. Chairman, whether the item of $60,000 for breakwater repairs for Souris harbour was passed or not, but in any case I am sure that the minister will answer my question. Is it the intention of the department this year to see that proper accommodation shall be provided for the transfer of goods from the railway to the steamer, especially the government subsidized steamer for the Magdalen islands? The accommodation at the transfer shed is unsatisfactory now owing to a leaky roof and other defects. Will anything be done this year to remedy that condition?
There is nothing in the estimates providing especially for that, but there is the general vote for work of that kind, and it is a little larger than usual this year.

I hope the minister will keep the condition of that shed in mind, because it is a very important one. I hope that something will be done in this direction out of the general vote so that the accommodation will be made of some real use to the people. It is of importance in several ways, and particularly because the Dominion government subsidizes a steamship service there to the amount of $50,000 a year, anad surely when a steamship service is subsidized to that extent the transfer shed from the railways to the steamer should be such as to afford protection to the goods.

Item agreed to.
Westville-wharf, $10,600.
I wonder where Westville is.
Does my hon. friend not know the location? For his information I may say that it is Queens county on the south side of the West river.

It is rather difficult to understand why so much money is voted for these places. There is a vote of $8,200 for wharf reconstruction and extension at West river bridge, and this vote of $10,600 for the wharf at Westville. Can the minister tell us just what business is being done at these places to justify such an expenditure?

The district engineer reports:
Westville is a point on the south side of the West river about five miles from Charlottetown, where a small structure known as "MeEwan's" wharf was built by the local government many years ago. It supplies shipping accommodation for the various communities in this vicinity, namely. New Dominion, Long Creek, Canoe Cove, South Shore, Nine Mile Creek and Fair-view, same containing probably from 600 to 800 persons interested in the export of surplus farm produce and import of coal, lumber and general merchandise by -water, as they are entirely cut off from any railway service. The wharf is also a point of call twice weekly for the subsidized steamer "Harland", but owing to recent development in the seed potato industry it has been found inadequate and vessels arriving in the busy shipping season have often to lie at the pierhead one outside the other. There are no statistics available as to the value of the business transacted over this wharf, but from personal observation covering the past twenty years or more I am of the opinion this would not exceed $50,000 per season. The wharf is still controlled by the local government, and as only small repairs have been made on it from time to time it is now in very bad condition and will shortly require to be entirely reconstructed. Under these circumstances shippers and others interested in obtaining improved facilities at the place desire that the present wharf be abandoned and an entirely new one built a short distance to the eastward, and I have no hesitation in advising the department that I consider that it would be better in every way to comply with such request. The proposed new site has an excellent approach both from water and land, with sufficient space for any warehouse accommodation that might eventually be required, while approach to present wharf is up a very steep hill, difficult to team heavy loads over, and the land surrounding it is neither available or suitable for the traffic that it is anticipated will follow improved shipping facilities at Westville.
2042	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-P.EJ.
Is that report from the district engineer?

Yes, the district engineer,
Mr. Hyndman.

I have a
great real of confidence in any report made by the district engineer, as I know he is a really practical man. How far is this wharf from the West river bridge wharf, for which there is a vote of over $8,000?

My information is that
it is three or four miles below that bridge.

When those
of us who know the situation existing there compare the treatment the West river is receiving with that accorded to other points in the province, especially in Kings county, we cannot help wondering why it is that so much attention is given to certain points, two, three or four miles apart in one county, and no attention whatever to large sections in another county.
It is well represented.

I was going to suggest, when my hon. friend interrupted, that the representation apparently has a great deal to do with it, and I say that with all due deference to my hon. friends from Queens county. My hon. friend (Mr. McPhee) lived alongside the West river a few years ago before he moved west, and he knows as well as I do that the expenditure of fifteen or twenty thousand dollars on sections of the river there three or four miles apart is justified by the exigencies of the representatives of Queens county.

Item agreed to.
Bailey's Brook-extension to pier, $3,000.

Mr. Chairman, what is
this item for?

This amount is required
to construct a cribwork extension 240 feet long, 10 feet wide and 10 feet high to the eastern pier. An extension to the pier is required in order to straighten and constrict the channel, thus preventing the accumulation of debris which obstructs the traffic. About sixty fishing boats use this harbour during the fishing season, and the improvement suggested will be of great benefit to them in the handling of their fish. The annual value of the fisheries is $24,500. Three lobster factories are located in the district, which has a population of approximately five hundred.
How much was spent last year, and who was the superintendent under whom the work was done?

Last year we spent $2,490
I have not the name of the superintendent. I shall be very glad to get it for my hon. friend.

Can the minister tell
me under whose recommendation the superintendent was appointed, and if he continued throughout the season to carry on the work?

I could not answer that
question offhand.

I think the minister had
better let the item stand over until he has the information ready.
It would facilitate matters if my hon. friend saw fit to let the item pass, but I am not going to urge it. I will undertake to supply all the information >he requires.

Will you allow me to
discuss the matter later?

Certainly, I shall be very
glad to.
With that understanding, all right.

Item agreed to.
Barrington passage-ice piers, $35,000.

Would the minister explain
on whose recommendation this is being done, and for what purpose?

Seventeen thousand dollars of this is a revote from last year. The amount is asked to be provided towards the construction of a second concrete pier at Barrington passage. The amount expended on the pier last year was only $104.

They are ice piers. What
purpose do they serve?

It is claimed that under
existing conditions the people of Cape Sable island are practically isolated during the winter months. The ferry which runs between Barrington passage and Cape Sable island cannot give regular service on account of the heavy ice fields which run up and down the passage making navigation unsafe. If the proposed piers were constructed across the passage they would keep the ice fields broken up in such small quantities that the ferry boats would have no difficulty in making daily trips.

Does this represent the final expenditure, or will further piers be necessary?

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-P.E.I.

It depends to a certain
extent upon the results obtained. If the first two piers constructed have the effect of doing what the engineer thinks they will do, it is possible that something further along that line will be done.
How much more?

There are only two piers
at the present time.

What is the final scheme if
this experiment proves satisfactory?
The $35,000 includes everything contemplated at the present time.

The present expenditure is
experimental, I understand?
Largely.

If the experiment proves
successful what is to be done further? Is there no definite scheme?

No, this is experimental
and there will be nothing definitely decided upon until the engineers have an opportunity of seeing how it works out.

On whose recommendation,
may I ask, is it being done?
The engineer's.

Is the minister quite sure?
I was informed that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) promised this work.

Yes, it is the engineer.
Part of his recommendation is as follows:
Under existing conditions, it is readily seen that the people of Cape Sable Island are practically isolated during the winter months, and the reason for this isolation is that the heavy ice fields which run up and down the passage do not allow the safe navigation of the passage, and it seems reasonable to believe that if ice piers were constructed across the passage at its narrowest part they would break the ice fields which flow back and forward through the passage during the winter. As the tide runs in and out of the passage four times a day. ice piers would no doubt keep the ice fields broken up in such small quantities that the ferry boats _ would have no difficulty in making their daily trips.
Is it being done on the recommendation of the Minister of National Defence? It is in his constituency.

I know he has spoken on
behalf of this.

Before the engineers made
their report?

I think it was after the
engineers reported.

Item agreed to.
Brooklyn-dredging, The Mersey Paper Company. Limited, to contribute one third of cost, $70,000.

The minister might
explain this item. There is another one of a similar character.

This is one of a number
of similar projects which the government have been assisting. This amount of $70,000 is asked to be provided towards the following dredging at North Brooklyn, the Mersey Paper Company Limited to contribute one-third of cost: The work proposed at Brooklyn consists of the dredging of a dock and basin for the pier of the Mersey Paper Mill Company. The average dimensions of this work are approximately; length, 1,150 feet; width, 550 feet; depth, 23.1 feet below L.W.OjS.T. It is estimated that 176,400 cubic yards scow measurement of sand, clay and gravel will have to be removed.
The object of the work is to provide suitable berths and basin to accommodate large steamers which will be engaged in carrying the products of The Mersey Paper Mill.

Will this wharf remain
under the control of the government?
No.
Is $70,000 the total cost, or will it be $105,000?

The total cost will be
$110,000. Our information is that The Mersey Company are expending a large sum of money there, variously estimated between six and nine million dollars, in establishing a paper mill at North Brooklyn; and I believe their power development will involve a further expenditure.

The power development is
being done by the provincial government entirely, but the company have built their plant and pier there at their own expense.

The government has
nothing to do with the pier?
No.

Who will have access
to the pier?

All those doing business
with this large concern; it is not a public pier.

How far is the government going to go with this policy. It is ridiculous to do dredging in connection with private piers.
2044	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Nova Scotia

It is the same policy as is followed in connection with dredging up to grain elevators. It is the policy of the government wherever there is a large expenditure of this kind creating considerable business development to endeavour to assist either in dredging or sometimes in actual dock construction. In this case we are assisting merely in the dredging.

Will the government
endeavour to secure from the company the right of access to the pier on the part of the public?
The government have done so in cases where they have contributed towards the wharf. But where they are doing only dredging I do not recall any case in which that right has been sought.
It seems to me that the public should have the right to use the wharf. This was the case in connection with Anticosti island.
Yes; but in that particular case additional construction was made to render the place a port of refuge.
Would it not be a good policy, wherever the government undertake to do dredging in connection with such operations as this, to provide that the public shall have the right to use the wharf?

I do not think that any
question in particular arises in connection with the matter. Practically everyone who will have any business at the wharf is doing business with The Mersey Company, and I know of no objection on their part to such persons using the wharf. What applies in some oases does not apply here. There is a very large development in this case and I understand that a substantial investment is being made by the company. In making arrangements in a matter of this kind you try as nearly as possible to do the fair thing in view of what the company has done. I think we are getting all that we are entitled to.

It might happen, however, that a town would grow up on this site and someone might want to build a store or to do business of any other nature, and it would be very inconvenient if they could not land material at the wharf without first obtaining the consent of the company. When the government does dredging of this sort it should receive, it seems to me, something in the nature of a quid pro quo. Personally I see no reason why the public should not be allowed to use the wharf.

In this particular district,
which happens to be in my constituency, this wharf is not required for public purposes. There is an excellent public wharf owned by the government.

There are two other
wharves.

Yes, there is a breakwater
and there is a wharf in the district. There is mo question about the public needing this wharf, for there is ample accommodation. Furthermore, dredging is always done to improve someone's waterfront or to render someone's wharf more accessible.
Is there a company town growing up there?
No, not do any extent.

Item agreed to.
Digby-repairs and renewals to pier, $6,000.

Has the minister had any
application with reference to dredging in Digby basin? He is aware, I presume, that Digby is the only entrance which the Canadian Pacific Railway have to Nova Scotia; that is to say, by steamer from St. John across to Digby. They have just given a contract for a very much larger steamer than is operating at the present time, an up to date vessel which will cost a considerable sum of money. This new vessel will draw very much more water than does the present boat, and it is absolutely necessary that dredging shall have been done by the time the boat arrives. Her construction will require about a year and it will take some time to do the dredging. I am wondering whether the minister has had any application from the town of Digby or from the Canadian Pacific Railway with reference to the necessity for dredging there.

In the details I have here ;here is nothing touching the matter to which ray hon. friend refers. Of course, we are only supplied with the details of the items actually in the estimates. It is just possible that such a request has been made but neither my deputy nor myself has it in mind at the moment.

I want to direct attention to the fact that this work will be absolutely necessary. The steamer now being built by the Canadian Pacific Railway for that service is 350 feet long, whereas the one now in use is less than 200 feet in length, so some extra dredging will be necessary. I do not ask this for the benefit of Digby at all but for the benefit of Canada generally, because this

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Nova Scotia
is the only Canadian Pacific Railway connection into Nova Scotia. I want to direct attention to the fact that some provision should be made in the dredging operations for the coming summer to take care of the necessary dredging at Digby basin because, with the present channel, at low tide this new steamer would be hardly able to turn round. As the minister knows, we have a great rise and fall of tides there; the average is 24 feet, and sometimes we have tides of 28 or 29 feet, so it is essential that this dredging should be done this summer.

I understand this is a
Canadian Pacific Railway steamer to which my hon. friend refers, and evidently at the time they were making this request they overlooked the work he has in mind. However,
I will be glad to have the matter looked into.
They gave the contract for the new ship only two or three weeks ago.

Item agreed to.
Fourehu-harbour improvements-The British Metals Corporation (Canada) to contribute one-third of cost, $75,000.
Is this also for dredging?
I would like an explanation of the work intended to be done at this point.

This amount is required for dredging at this point; The British Metals Corporation (Canada) is to contribute one-third of the cost. It is proposed to dredge the entrance channel generally 100 feet wide and 2,050 feet, long, to a grade of 16 feet, with a turning basin at Cann's Point 600 feet long and 100 feet to 300 feet wide to the same depth. Through the rock area at the outer end of the channel, which is 700 feet long, it is proposed to limit the bottom width of the dredging to 75 feet. The completion of this channel and basin will provide for vessels of 17 to 20 feet draft and will give ample accommodation for local coastal vessels.

What
were the reports from the engineers? What class of dredging is it to be?

District Engineer Locke
requested this appropriation, and according to his statement The British Metals Corporation (Canada), in their letter of April 10, 1928 to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, requested consideration by the department of the provision of shipping facilities for them in order that they might proceed with the
shipping of concentrates produced from ore from their mines at Stirling, Richmond county, Nova Scotia. The company followed this up by their letters of August 17 and October 11, 1928, and their telegrams of October 26 and 31, 192S. There was also a telegram on January 21, 1929, from Mr. M. A. Patterson of Sydney, Nova Scotia, and Hon. J. L. Ralston also wrote in respect of this matter in May of last year.
I asked about the dredging. What have the engineers reported as to the class of material to be removed, and what kind of harbour do they thing they can make?

I gave my hon. friend the size of the harbour, its length, depth and width. It is estimated that the rock excavation will amount to 16,000 cubic yards, place measurement, estimated to cost $8 per yard, and it is estimated that the dredging will amount to 186,000 cubic yards, at 50 cents per yard.
Is this $75,000 the total cost or two-thirds of the cost?
The total cost to complete the work will be about $200,000, and this is one-half of our contribution.

Then the government
will pay $150,000 altogether?
Yes.

How
does the government propose to do the dredging at the entrance to the channel?
What does my hon. friend mean; does he mean by contract or day labour?

How is
it proposed to remove the stone in the entrance? I have gone over this location very carefully; I was with the engineer when this harbour was inspected in 1926, and we found that the entrance was solid stone. How does the government intend to remove this stone?
I think the ordinary practice will be followed, so far as I know; they will drill and blast and then take out the stone with a dipper dredge.

They will drill and blast
and then claim extras.

No doubt they will claim everything they can.
2046	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Nova Scotia

Is this
work to be done by contract or by day labour?

I think it will be done
by contract.

In Nova Scotia we have found in the past that most of these contractors come back for extras. This will be a very expensive work if it is done by tender and contract, and I think it is up to the government to safeguard themselves in some way. A short time ago we had the case of St. Peter's canal; I notice that in the estimates this year we are providing an amount for 1925 extras.

Might I ask if this
is a new harbour we are creating or if shipping has used this harbour previously?

Fishing boats and small
coastal boats have used the harbour for some time but up to the present it has not been an improved harbour.

For the benefit of the hon. member for Mackenzie I may say that Fourchu is an old harbour. We have 12 feet of water there, but extensive developments are made necessary through the increased shipping which will result from the mines at Stirling. Fourchu as a harbour was frequented as early as 1700.
Before this item carries I would like to thank the Minister of Public Works for the magnificent way in which he has treated the county of Richmond. I notice that there are a few other points which he has treated in a very substantial manner but the only way we can get action from the minister is to go after him as hard as we possibly can. I am very glad to see that he has remembered my old constituency in the way he has.
I understand that requests have been made on many occasions from the district of Main a Dieu, asking that a shed be placed on the public wharf there. I understand that the fisherman's union have sent a request that this should be built. The wharf was built in 1925 and the fishermen of the district have asked for a shed. The cost of building this shed would not be very much and it would be of great convenience to the fishermen.
I would like also to direct the minister's attention to the need of a public wharf at Louisburg. This is the oldest town in the province of Nova Scotia and is one of the larger towns in the province. It is without a public wharf and I claim that it is a disgrace for the government to allow this community to go this length of time without 
having such a public convenience. I would ask the minister to forget some of his friends in that district. The reason a public wharf has not been built is that his friends have secured options on all the available property in that district, and the minister is not in a position to decide which one he is going to purchase the property from.
Are they good friends or bad friends?

I do not think they are good friends, when they do a thing of that kind. I would ask the minister to take this matter under immediate consideration.
Another matter requiring immediate attention is the repairing of the breakwater at Gabarouse. I understand that some of the logs required for the purpose have been taken to the district of Fourchu and the breakwater at Gabarouse, which is badly in need of repairs, must be allowed to go by the board.

Item agreed to.
Glace Bay-wharf reconstruction, $16,000.
I am very glad indeed to see this vote in the estimates. Could the minister tell the house if that wharf has been taken over by the government?
The negotiations are nearly completed but the agreement has not actually been signed.
It will be taken over?
That is the intention.
The intention is that this vote will be spent this year and not revoted next year.
That is getting into the realm of prophecy to a large extent. The completion of the agreement has taken a longer time than we contemplated and that is :he reason for the revote this year.
The terms have all been agreed on?
Yes, but it is impossible to say how long it will be before the agreement is completed. The work will not be started until that agreement is contemplated but I expect that it will be done this year.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Nova Scotia
Grass Cove-breakwater wharf, $2,000.
